issues.description: The UML in the problem statement defines Animal with two attributes (name: String and age: int) and a constructor Animal(String, int), but the provided solution implements Animal with only a name and a single-argument constructor Animal(String). This mismatch between the UML and the solution (and the template's implicit expectations) can confuse students about which constructor and attributes they must implement.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the specification and template consistent. Either (A) update the UML and textual description to remove the age attribute and require Animal(String) (so Animal has only name), or (B) update the template/solution to include the age attribute and a constructor Animal(String, int) plus corresponding getter/setter for age. Ensure examples and Main comments reflect the chosen constructor signature.

issues.description: The problem statement's UML and instructions specify that Animal has an 'age' attribute and a constructor Animal(String, int), but the provided solution and template use a single-argument constructor (Animal(String)) and omit the 'age' attribute. This mismatch between the problem specification and code artifacts creates confusion about the Animal entity's expected attributes and constructor signature and may mislead students when mapping the UML/tasks to the implementation or when tests expect the two-argument constructor.
issues.suggestedFix: Either update the solution and template to match the UML/spec by adding a private int age field and a constructor Animal(String, int) (and adapt all subclass constructors and example usages to pass an age), or revise the problem statement/UML to remove the 'age' attribute and specify a single-argument constructor consistently. Ensure all three artifacts use the same Animal attribute list and constructor signature.
